title: Root Disk Full on a Server With No App Data
intro: A small gateway server with barely any application data hit 100% disk. Services are crashing because they can't write temp files.

steps.fake_output:
Filesystem  Size  Used  Avail  Use%  Mounted on
/dev/sda1    20G   20G     0   100%  /

steps.prompt: Find which top-level directory under /var is biggest.
steps.hint: Narrow down where the space went.

steps.prompt: Almost all of it is logs. Check how much the systemd journal specifically is using.
steps.fake_output: Archived and active journals take up 15.6G in the file system.

steps.prompt: Find which service is producing the most log volume today.
expected_commands: journalctl --since today -o json | jq -r '._SYSTEMD_UNIT' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
journalctl --since today | awk '{print $5}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
steps.hint: The count-per-source pipeline from the Linux tutorials works here too.

steps.prompt: gateway-proxy is logging every single request at debug level. Free space immediately by shrinking the journal to 1GB.
steps.fake_output: Vacuuming done, freed 14.6G of archived journals from /var/log/journal.
steps.hint: vacuum-size limits total size; vacuum-time limits age.

resolution: A proxy service had been left at debug log level, emitting a line per request — millions per day — and journald's default size cap (10% of the filesystem, up to 4GB) had been overridden in journald.conf during an earlier debugging session and never restored. Vacuuming restored service immediately. Permanent fixes: set SystemMaxUse=1G in /etc/systemd/journald.conf (and restart systemd-journald), return the proxy to info-level logging, and alert on root disk usage at 80%. This is the monitoring-category twin of linux-incident-002: logs are one of the most common causes of full disks, and log volume itself is worth watching.
